Your First C++ Program
To get a feel of what C++ code looks like, let's write our first C++ program.
We will write a simple Hello, World! program.
Example
Don't worry about the code. For now, just press the "Run Code" button to execute the code.
If you get Hello, World! as output, congratulations, you have successfully run your first program!
The code above provides the basic structure of a C++ program. Let's now briefly understand this structure.
How does it work?
Use this space for your doubts about this lesson. Ask us anything that's confusing and our experts will provide explanations to help you understand.

Kelish Rai from Programiz

I assume this is your first time seeing a C++ code snippet, and I completely understand if it feels a bit overwhelming. But let me make it clear that we don't expect you to understand everything line by line at this stage.
Instead of stressing about every detail, I recommend continuing through the course. As you progress, these concepts will start making more sense.
That said, here’s a quick breakdown of the code:

items: #include <iostream> includes the iostream library in your program, which allows you to use functions like std::cout and std::cin.
using namespace std; allows you to use cout and cin without typing std:: every time, making the code cleaner.
int main() is the main function, where the program starts executing.
cout << "Hello World!"; prints "Hello World!" to the output screen.
return 0; marks the end of the main() function and returns 0, indicating that the program ran successfully.

Abhilekh Gautam from Programiz
#include <iostream> is used to include the iostream library in your program. By including this, you gain access to cout, which allows you to display output on the screen.
Don’t worry if this feels a bit unfamiliar right now, it’s a fundamental concept in C++, and you’ll dive deeper into how and why it’s used in the upcoming chapters.
